adapted_prompts.title: Context interview
adapted_prompts.use: Use before a new project; attach the actual files or appshot.
adapted_prompts.prompt: I want to build [outcome] in my Windows Codex workspace. The intended user is [who], and the important constraints are [constraints]. Inspect the available files, tools and attached context first. Ask only questions whose answers would materially change the design; continue independent work while waiting. Give me a small first milestone with observable acceptance criteria, then implement it. Use a browser in the background for inspection; do not put it in full screen.

adapted_prompts.title: Turn a screen into a brief
adapted_prompts.use: Use an appshot plus your spoken or typed intent.
adapted_prompts.prompt: From this attached appshot and my notes, recover the intended workflow, data inputs, visible controls and missing decisions. Separate what you can actually see from inference. Build the smallest useful version for Windows. Before calling it complete, run it and exercise the main user path. Return the artifact, the check result and any remaining limitation.

adapted_prompts.title: Make a repository assembly manual
adapted_prompts.use: The closest replication of the video’s IKEA example.
adapted_prompts.prompt: Inspect this repository and its current documentation. Produce one self-contained HTML assembly manual in an IKEA instruction style: monochrome line diagrams, a parts list, numbered panels, connection arrows and a final assembled view. Explain the actual entry points, data flow, optional components and failure boundaries. Link each technical claim to the relevant file or official documentation. Mark inferred relationships. Check the diagrams against the implementation and render the HTML. Do not add features to the repository.

adapted_prompts.title: Choose and verify the action surface
adapted_prompts.use: Useful for browser QA and dashboard work.
adapted_prompts.prompt: Task: [specific browser outcome]. First identify which available tool can do it and where the relevant session is signed in. Prefer structured tools when available; otherwise use the isolated browser for local/public content or my signed-in Chrome for the named service. Keep inspection in the background. Verify the final visible state and save evidence. If the task requires foreground Windows desktop control, explain the concrete need before starting it.

adapted_prompts.title: Export data with a contract
adapted_prompts.use: Make the time window and schema explicit.
adapted_prompts.prompt: From [dashboard], export [metric] as CSV for [start inclusive] through [end exclusive], using timezone [zone], and [other metric] as JSON for [period]. Preserve the source’s filters and document them. Verify headers, row counts, date boundaries, units and totals against the visible source. Save both outputs locally with an export note. Report missing data rather than filling it in.

adapted_prompts.title: Document → draft form
adapted_prompts.use: Adapt the demonstrated transfer to your own questions.
adapted_prompts.prompt: Read [named document] and create a draft form in [named service] using its questions. Preserve wording, choices, order and required status. Check the editor and respondent preview, including invalid submission and one valid test response if a disposable test is available. Report the resulting draft link and discrepancies. Keep it a draft; publication is outside this task.

adapted_prompts.title: Set a verifiable goal
adapted_prompts.use: Invoke /goal in a supported client, then supply this contract.
adapted_prompts.prompt: Goal: [observable outcome]. Constraints: [scope, budget, platforms, prohibited changes]. Keep one active milestone and durable GOALS.md notes covering acceptance criteria, evidence, decisions, next actions and blockers. Complete the milestone only when its checks pass. If workers help, give each an independent scope and integrate their evidence. After a milestone, reconcile the documentation with the actual code and choose the next bounded milestone.

adapted_prompts.title: Replicate a paper rigorously
adapted_prompts.use: Designed for a research workbench, not a claim of automatic discovery.
adapted_prompts.prompt: Reproduce [specific claim or algorithm] from [paper/version/pages] on [dataset or small synthetic instances]. First record assumptions, objective, constraints, units, conventions and the exact claim. Establish a simple reference implementation and independent small-instance oracle where feasible. Compare outputs with tolerances justified by the method. Separate implementation correctness, empirical reproduction and theoretical guarantees. Preserve seeds, dependencies, commands and failures. Do not call a heuristic result globally optimal without a valid certificate or proof.

adapted_prompts.title: Delegate one bounded job
adapted_prompts.use: Use only when the main task actually benefits from a subagent.
adapted_prompts.prompt: Use a subagent for [independent task] with ownership of [files/responsibility]. Acceptance evidence: [check or artifact]. It is not alone in the codebase: it must preserve others’ edits and accommodate concurrent work. Give it the relevant context, an explicit stopping condition and the facts it must report. Keep integration and final verification with the main agent. Reuse an existing suitable worker before creating another.

adapted_prompts.title: Coordinate visible chats
adapted_prompts.use: This explicitly authorizes the named coordination.
adapted_prompts.prompt: Coordinate these existing Codex chats: [exact titles or IDs]. You may send each the scoped instructions needed for [specific project purpose]. Assign non-overlapping ownership, use worktrees where independent code changes require isolation, and maintain a short dashboard of owner, scope, last evidence, next action and blockers. Report integrated results after checking them; an idle worker alone is not proof of success.

adapted_prompts.title: Interrogate progress
adapted_prompts.use: Use a supported side conversation, or ask in the main chat.
adapted_prompts.prompt: What changed in the last working interval? What evidence supports the current status? What is on the critical path, what can proceed independently, and what exact input would unblock you? Answer concisely, then continue the authorized work. Put any durable decision back into the project’s main notes.

adapted_prompts.title: Audit before accepting completion
adapted_prompts.use: Ask for a fresh review perspective when justified.
adapted_prompts.prompt: Audit this milestone against its acceptance criteria and the actual artifact. Look for contradictions between implementation, tests, dashboard, README and reported guarantees. Exercise the important failure paths. For every finding give severity, concrete evidence and the smallest fix. After fixes, rerun the affected checks and state exactly what remains unverified.

adapted_prompts.title: Make one repeated check deterministic
adapted_prompts.use: No need for an elaborate hook framework.
adapted_prompts.prompt: The repeated step is [specific repository check]. Inspect my installed Codex version and existing hook configuration. Implement the smallest Windows-compatible deterministic command, with an appropriate timeout and useful failure output. Run it manually first. Then configure the appropriate lifecycle hook without overwriting unrelated hooks. Verify when it runs and demonstrate its failure and success behavior.

adapted_prompts.title: Monitor this task to completion
adapted_prompts.use: Use the app’s automation tool; do not emulate it with raw cron text.
adapted_prompts.prompt: Monitor [named ongoing task/process] every [interval] until [observable completion or stop condition]. Continue only work already authorized for this task. Stay quiet while state is unchanged or non-actionable; notify on meaningful progress, completion, failure or a specific required input. Record evidence of completion and remove or disable the monitor when done. Keep external messages, spending and access changes within my explicitly stated scope.

adapted_prompts.title: Build a bounded feedback loop
adapted_prompts.use: Start with triage; expand only after it works.
adapted_prompts.prompt: For [named feedback source] and [named repository], create a first pass that reads new items, deduplicates them and classifies bug, feature request, question or compliment. For actionable bugs, reproduce the issue and prepare a scoped fix in an isolated worktree with relevant checks and a draft PR. You may message [specific recipient/channel] only for [specific purpose], if supplied here. Keep a ledger so repeated runs do not duplicate issues or PRs. Stop at the defined scope boundary and report uncertain cases.

adapted_prompts.title: Save the workflow that actually worked
adapted_prompts.use: Run after a successful manual task.
adapted_prompts.prompt: Extract a reusable skill from this completed workflow. Include when to use it, required inputs, available tools, steps, evidence checks, known failure modes and the scope of authorized side effects. Generalize the procedure without retaining private data or project-specific credentials. Prefer instructions; add a script only for a deterministic step that benefits from one. Validate the skill and exercise it on one new example.

adapted_prompts.title: Build a minimal App Server client
adapted_prompts.use: An optional developer track after the operator loop is reliable.
adapted_prompts.prompt: Build a minimal Windows-compatible client for the Codex App Server version installed here. Generate or inspect that version’s protocol schema first. Demonstrate initialization, thread creation, one turn, streamed events, interruption and reconnection or resume where supported. Handle approval requests explicitly and keep the listener local. Use a simple interface; add custom styling after the lifecycle works. Show one runnable end-to-end check and document unsupported behavior.

excluded_evidence: Automated scene analysis with incomplete coverage and inconsistent timing
validation_boundary: HTML rendering and interactions can be checked; workflows in prompts were not executed for this guide.

source_prompts.title: Build from an appshot
source_prompts.text: Hey, can you just build this?
source_prompts.context: Charlie attaches a Slack appshot describing the translation app. The six-word request works because the attachment carries the specification; the build response is not part of the prompt. Spoken at 07:32, visible in the follow-up inspection at 07:45.

source_prompts.title: Explain a repository as an IKEA manual
source_prompts.text: Can you create a visualization of this repository in the style of an IKEA instruction manual? I want to understand how all of the primitives fit together.
source_prompts.context: Charlie supplies the repository context. Wording follows the auto-generated captions; punctuation and fillers are normalized. This is a request for component relationships, assembly and understanding.

source_prompts.title: Export dashboard data
source_prompts.text: Hey, can you help me download the number of commits for the last seven days as a CSV and the pull request data as a JSON from the start of the month to today? Use computer use and go for it.
source_prompts.context: Gabriel supplies the dashboard appshot. A repeated phrase is removed. The demonstration later clarifies 1–29 June 2026 for the pull-request period; “today” belongs to that historical session. Use explicit dates in a fresh run.

source_prompts.title: Turn document questions into a feedback form
source_prompts.text: Hey, can you create this feedback form for me using the questions in the Google Docs? Remember to mark each question as mandatory.
source_prompts.context: Gabriel attaches the source document context and selects Chrome. Fillers and the spoken restart are removed. Required status is an explicit acceptance condition.

source_prompts.title: Build a live audience Q&A site
source_prompts.text:
I want you to build a live audience Q&A site for talks and fireside chats. It should be polished enough to use at a real event and comfortably support 400 people in the same session, including bursts of submissions and votes.

The admin should be able to configure a session to collect questions, topic suggestions, or both. Participants should get a very simple mobile experience where they can submit something, browse approved submissions, and upvote what they most want discussed. A participant can upvote each submission once and remove that vote later. Rankings and vote counts should update in real time without a refresh.
source_prompts.context: These are the first two complete visible paragraphs, transcribed from the screen. Three attached mockups cover stage display, participant mobile view and admin dashboard. The longer prompt continues into moderation, duplicate merging and AI tags/clusters; the displayed final paragraph is clipped, so this is not the full brief. The host says this presentation version was polished from earlier dictation.

source_prompts.title: Run the Optimal Trees project through milestones
source_prompts.text:
Ask any questions that would materially change the architecture or scope. If something is non-blocking, state the assumption and continue.

## How I want you to run the project

Use this main thread as the orchestrator. Its job is to maintain the plan and source of truth, choose the next goal, delegate work, integrate evidence, and keep me informed. Apart from small coordination edits, it should not read all the papers itself, write the package, run the full benchmarks, or perform the reviews. Put substantive research, implementation, testing, benchmarking, documentation, and packaging work into well-scoped sub-agents or separate threads.

At the start, invoke [Define Goal] and create a GOALS.md file with several milestone-based goals and a clear, verifiable definition of done for each. Keep only one milestone active at a time. When it is complete, blocked, or no longer the right next step, use [Define Goal] again to choose or sharpen the next active goal. Keep GOALS.md honest and current, with concrete evidence for completed milestones and a clear record of what remains.

Create a simple, clean progress-dashboard.html early in the project and keep it current throughout the run.
source_prompts.context: The excerpt begins after a clipped earlier section and ends before a dashboard requirements list. [Define Goal] represents the visible tool chips, not literal typed brackets. The scientific package requirements preceding this orchestration section were not fully recovered. Multi-agent delegation is expressly requested here; it is not a rule for every project.

source_prompts.title: Create a series of goals
source_prompts.text: Hey, don't create one goal, create a series of goals and put it in a goals markdown file.
source_prompts.context: Gabriel describes the instruction behind the milestone workflow. The on-screen file is GOALS.md. The persistent series of milestones is distinct from the single currently active goal.

source_prompts.title: Ask a local thread to test remote work
source_prompts.text: Hey, you can spawn a local thread on my machine and use the Chrome extension to then inspect it.
source_prompts.context: Gabriel describes remote-to-local browser QA. The screen shows a delegated thread, but this short instruction comes from the narration. Local browser access depends on the available client and installed tools.

source_prompts.title: Send a concise progress report
source_prompts.text: Hey, reply to this thread and give me a summary of what's done, what's not yet done, and are there any blockers?
source_prompts.context: Gabriel describes using a Slack plugin and a named thread. Private thread/channel identifiers are omitted. This historical example does not authorize messages to any destination in a new run.

source_prompts.title: Ask what happened and what is next
source_prompts.text: Hey, what's going on? Can you list what you've done so far, maybe in the last hour? What do you plan to do next? Is there anything I can do to unblock you?
source_prompts.context: Gabriel dictates this in a side conversation. The hosts advise sending durable decisions back to the main thread because side conversations can become stale.

source_prompts.title: Choose the correct local QA project
source_prompts.text: Test spawning a local thread in the local FormBuilder project. If it succeeds, make that the default location for all future local threads, especially for Chrome or end-to-end testing.
source_prompts.context: The host reads the visible request aloud. Punctuation and a spoken restart are normalized; this is not an independently complete screen transcription. It tests the bridge before relying on it for QA.

source_prompts.title: Steer a weak UI result
source_prompts.status: Spoken report of a sent request
source_prompts.context: Gabriel reports sending this short criticism with a screenshot. The main agent agrees and messages an existing QA subagent. This is an example of screenshot context plus mid-task steering; specific defects and acceptance checks make a stronger reusable critique.

source_prompts.title: Read and classify channel feedback every half hour
source_prompts.text: Every half an hour, can you just like look at the comments and suggestions in this channel and reply to them? I think there'll be like a few categories. There's one category where it's like compliments, there's one category where it's a bug report, there's one category where it's a feature request, so forth.
source_prompts.context: The complete visible sentences are transcribed; the bubble ends with “Then we just like...” and is truncated. The attached channel appshot is essential context and is omitted here for privacy. A recurring check begins, but the complete eventual feedback-to-PR pipeline is not established on screen.

source_prompts.title: Steer feedback handling into a worktree and PR
source_prompts.text: If it's a bug fix or feature request, can you also spin a new thread in a worktree and actually address that, then open a PR and request [reviewer] to review it? Ask [reviewer] to approve it within 24 hours; if not, keep reminding them.
source_prompts.context: Fillers are removed and the named recipient is replaced with [reviewer]. Gabriel calls this a comical example. The request is issued while the earlier automation is still working; it is not evidence that every downstream action completed. Supply explicit recipients and sensible reminder limits before adapting it.

source_prompts.title: Monitor presentation pacing
source_prompts.text: Run an automation every five minutes, taking a screenshot of the Google Chrome presentation, and estimate whether we are going to overrun.
source_prompts.context: This is a concise reconstruction of Gabriel’s explanation, not an exact initial prompt. A later checkpoint is visible. The actual presentation deadline and schedule belong to the source session; specify yours in a new run.

source_prompts.title: Review skills and project instructions weekly
source_prompts.text: Every Friday, review my conversation threads for skills that could be improved, additions to AGENTS.md, and unused skills that could be removed.
source_prompts.context: Gabriel proposes this workflow; it is not demonstrated end-to-end. This text reconstructs the idea rather than quoting a sent prompt. Review suggested removals before changing a working collection.

source_prompts.title: Learn from the reply actually sent
source_prompts.text: Compare the drafted email reply with the eventual reply I sent, treating the sent reply as ground truth for my editing preferences. Update a Markdown file with best practices and tips for future drafts.
source_prompts.context: A proposed second automation, reconstructed from narration. “Ground truth” here concerns the user’s preferred final wording; it does not establish the factual correctness of an email. The video does not show this feedback loop being validated.

source_prompts.title: Ask about a workstream from accumulated notes
source_prompts.text: Hey, what's going on with the latest [workstream]?
source_prompts.context: Charlie describes a heartbeat that reads incoming updates and refreshes local Obsidian notes. The example phrase is incomplete in narration; [workstream] is a supplied placeholder, so this is not a complete verbatim prompt. The useful mechanism is maintaining context before asking a short question.

source_prompt_coverage: 18 recoverable visual or spoken requests and explicitly marked reconstructions; not all original prompt bodies are visible. Four entries transcribe complete visible wording or bounded excerpts; all other labels state normalization or reconstruction.
